issues.legal_issue: A possession suit by an unregistered firm against a former tenant is barred only to the extent it seeks to enforce a right arising from the expired lease, and an independent claim based on the former tenant’s legal duty to return possession may sustain the decree.
material_facts: The plaintiff firm was unregistered when it filed suit against the former tenant.
The lease had expired, and the former tenant remained in possession without becoming a tenant by holding over.
The plaint relied both on lease covenants requiring delivery of possession and on the legal duty to return possession after the lease ended.
There was no agreement permitting the former tenant to remain in possession after the lease ended.
The firm obtained registration while the suit was pending, but the Court found it unnecessary to decide whether that registration cured any initial defect.
issues.conclusion: The suit was barred in part because the contractual claim was brought by an unregistered firm, but the independent claim based on the legal duty to return possession was not barred. The decree for possession therefore remained sustainable, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 69(2) of the Partnership Act, an unregistered firm cannot sue a third party to enforce a right arising from a contract; the provision is mandatory and is strictly construed. A claim based on the independent legal duty to return possession following determination of a lease is not a contractual claim barred by that section. Sections 111(a) and 108(q) of the Transfer of Property Act provide respectively for determination by efflux of time and the lessee’s duty upon determination to put the lessor in possession, absent a contract to the contrary. The Court treated an ex-tenant remaining without the landlord’s assent as a tenant at sufferance, relying on Ganga Dutt Murarka v. Kartik Chandra Das, M.C. Chockalingam v. V. Manickayasagam, and R.V. Bhupal Prasad v. State of A.P.; it also relied on Madan Lal v. Bhai Anand Singh on the need for a contract to the contrary. In construing the plaint as a whole, the Court considered Udhav Singh v. Madhav Rao Scindia and Ram Sarup Gupta v. Bishun Narain Inter College. It distinguished Jagdish Chander Gupta v. Kajaria Traders (India) Ltd., which concerned enforcement of an arbitration agreement.

rule.if: unregistered_firm_sues_third_party and lease_expired_by_efflux and former_tenant_remains_without_holding_over and plaint_relies_on_surrender_covenant and plaint_also_relies_on_independent_return_duty and no_agreement_allows_continued_possession

predicates.unregistered_firm_sues_third_party: An unregistered firm brought suit against a person who was a third party to the firm.
predicates.lease_expired_by_efflux: The lease ended because its specified term ran out.
predicates.former_tenant_remains_without_holding_ov: The former tenant stayed in possession without the landlord’s assent to a continuing tenancy.
predicates.plaint_relies_on_surrender_covenant: The firm relied on a lease covenant requiring the tenant to deliver possession when the lease ended.
predicates.plaint_also_relies_on_independent_return: The firm also relied on a legal duty to return possession that did not depend on enforcing the lease covenant.
predicates.no_agreement_allows_continued_possession: The parties had no agreement allowing the former tenant to remain in possession after the lease ended.

issues.definition: When an unregistered firm sues a third party after a lease ends, relies both on a surrender covenant and on an independent return duty, and the former tenant remains without an agreement permitting continued possession, the contractual part is barred but the possession decree may be sustained on the independent ground.
